title: Requests decide placement
summary: The scheduler adds requests, not usage.

steps.n: A pod asks for one core and two gigabytes of memory.
Node A has 0.5 core unreserved, so it is filtered out even if it is idle.
Node B has two cores unreserved and passes the filter.
The scheduler binds the pod and counts its requests against node B.
The kubelet sets the cgroup shares from the CPU request.
The pod runs and can use idle CPU above its request until the node is busy.

title: Failure and recovery: an OOM kill
summary: A memory limit kills a container and a measured limit fixes it.

steps.n: A batch step loads a larger file and memory use rises past the limit.
The kernel kills the process at the cgroup limit with signal nine.
The kubelet restarts the container and the cycle repeats.
The engineer sees OOMKilled and exit code 137 in the pod description.
Metrics show a peak of 900 MiB against a 512 MiB limit.
They set the request to 700 MiB and the limit to 1 GiB.
Restarts stop and an alert watches memory use near the limit.

title: Failure and recovery: throttled latency
summary: Short bursts hit the CPU quota and latency rises.

steps.n: A request starts several threads at once.
The threads use the whole 100 ms quota in 20 ms of wall time.
The kernel pauses the container for the remaining 80 ms of the period.
Users see response times jump even though average CPU is low.
The engineer sees almost half of the periods are throttled.
They raise the CPU limit and keep the request near typical use.
The p99 response time falls back to its normal value.

title: A quota refuses a pod
summary: Admission stops a pod that would exceed the namespace quota.

steps.n: A ReplicaSet controller asks for a new pod with a 500m CPU request.
The quota already has 3.8 of 4 cores requested.
The sum would exceed the limit, so admission rejects the pod.
The controller records a FailedCreate event naming the quota.
The team reads the event and decides to right-size requests or ask for more quota.
After the change, pods are admitted and the scheduler places them.

title: Eviction under memory pressure
summary: The kubelet picks pods that exceed their requests first.

steps.n: Available memory falls below the eviction threshold.
The kubelet marks the node with memory pressure and stops new pods.
It evicts the pod with no requests because it is first in the order.
If still low, it evicts the burstable pod using the most memory above its request.
The guaranteed pod is kept unless system daemons are in danger.
Memory recovers and the pressure condition is removed.

title: Failure and recovery: eviction storm
summary: Missing reservations let pods starve the kubelet.

steps.n: Pods with large limits use almost all memory on the node.
The kubelet and runtime compete for memory and respond slowly.
The node stops reporting in time and is marked NotReady.
The operator finds no kube or system reserved memory is configured.
They set kube reserved and system reserved and an eviction threshold.
An alert is added for memory pressure and eviction counts.
Pods are evicted in order before the kubelet is affected.

title: One autoscaling decision
summary: The HPA compares usage with a target.

steps.n: Average CPU across pods is 90 percent of requests.
With a 60 percent target and 4 pods the result is 4 times 90 over 60, rounded up to 6.
The scale up is allowed at once and a scale down would wait for the stabilization window.
The HPA writes 6 replicas to the Deployment.
The scheduler places two new pods if there is capacity.
Average CPU drops toward 60 percent as load spreads.

title: Failure and recovery: HPA unknown
summary: Missing requests stop autoscaling until they are added.

steps.n: Traffic doubles and the pods slow down.
The HPA asks the metrics server for CPU use of the pods.
Usage is returned but there is no request to measure a percentage against.
The HPA reports unknown and keeps the replica count unchanged.
The engineer reads the HPA conditions and sees a missing request message.
They add CPU requests based on measured usage to the Deployment.
The HPA calculates a target and raises replicas.
The recommender reads weeks of CPU and memory use.
It reports a target request below the current one for most containers.
The engineer checks that a monthly peak is not missing from the history.
They update the Deployment requests with extra headroom.
Pods restart with the new requests and fit on fewer nodes.
Throttling and OOM metrics stay flat after the change.

title: Node autoscaling for pending pods
summary: New nodes appear when pods cannot fit.

steps.n: Six pods stay Pending because no node has free requests.
The autoscaler sees unschedulable pods and simulates adding a node.
It asks the cloud for one more node from the right group.
The machine starts, joins the cluster and becomes Ready.
The scheduler places the pending pods on the new node.
When the node is empty for a while it is drained and removed.

title: A drain respects a budget
summary: Evictions pause when the budget would be broken.

steps.n: A drain asks the API server to evict one pod of the app.
The budget requires two available and three are running, so one may go.
The pod is evicted and removed gracefully.
The drain asks again before the new pod is ready.
Only two are available now, so the eviction is refused and the drain waits.
The scheduler places the replacement, the budget allows again and the drain continues.

title: Failure and recovery: a zone fails
summary: Spread and spare capacity keep the service up.

steps.n: Six replicas are spread two in each zone by a topology constraint.
The nodes in zone A become unreachable.
The scheduler tries to place the two lost replicas in the other zones.
Zones B and C have spare requests for them, so both fit.
The operator sees six ready replicas and normal latency.
They note that without spare capacity the replicas would have stayed Pending.
A whole-zone drain is added to the quarterly game day.
